catalog_quote: Classical Nahuatl and nearly all modern dialects are described as having a fixed penultimate stress accent ... We hypothesize that, in what is a historically fixed stress accent language, tone has developed as a reflex of a breathy coda segment in two subdialects of Nahuatl spoken along the Balsas River: Oapan, where the segment has been lost, and Ahuelicán, where the segment has been maintained. ... The varieties of Nahuatl studied here also exhibit the word-prosodic feature found in other extant varieties of Nahuatl, which may be uncontroversially termed stress accent in either of the typologies reviewed here. As will be presented below, this accentual prominence is historically located on the penultimate syllable of the word, although in the two tonogenetic variants the locus of this stress accent may shift in words that have innovated tone. ... tone_statements.citation: Amith, Jonathan D. 2014. Tonogenesis and Reduplication in Balsas River Nahuatl of Central Guerrero, Mexico. Paper presented at the Workshop on the Sound Systems of Mexico and Central America (SSMCA), Yale University, New Haven, 4-6 April 2014. 2-pp. abstract.
tone_statements.quote: Several Nahuatl speaking communities in the Balsas River valley of central Guerrero, Mexico, have developed a hybrid stress and tone system from a breathy-voiced coda segment [ɦ], which has been shown to lower F0 in a tautosyllabic vowel, creating a H-L F0 contour beginning on the preceding syllable ... Ahuelican manifests the most conservative system: retention of *h which triggers a phonologized high-low F0 contour ... Oapan manifests what is hypothesized to be a more developed and fully tonal system. The trigger, *h, has been lost ... Tone and stress interact in a "clash avoidance" pattern, resulting in a rightward shift of the latter
tone_statements.locator: abstract p.1, opening paragraph and discussion of exx. 1-4
tone_statements.summary: Hybrid: penult stress accent + innovated lexical tone from coda *h/[ɦ]; Ahuelicán H-L contour (L specified), Oapan lexical H with stress-tone clash avoidance (moraic), Ameyaltepec/Tetelcingo no tone.

tone_statements.citation: Guion, Susan G., Jonathan D. Amith, Christopher Doty & Irina A. Shport. 2006. Production characteristics of accent in four dialects of Nahuatl. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 120(5, Suppl.): 3092 (4th joint ASA/ASJ meeting abstract).
tone_statements.quote: dialects from Guerrero state have been described with pitch-accent from historical coda breathy /h/ in nonfinal position ... Innovated pitch-accent was found to be cued solely by F0. Penultimate accent varied in its production by dialect. ... Dialects with innovated pitch-accent had less stresslike penultimate accents, being cued primarily by F0, or with a relatively small durational difference, but no voice quality difference. This indicates that the innovation of a pitch-accent has changed the formerly stresslike penultimate accent into a more pitch-type accent.
tone_statements.summary: Two Balsas dialects: innovated F0-only pitch accent from coda breathy /h/ beside penult accent; two dialects: penult stress accent only.

tone_statements.citation: Guion, Susan G. & Jonathan D. Amith. 2005. The effect of [h] on tonal development in Nahuatl. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 117(4, Suppl.): 2490 (149th ASA meeting abstract).
tone_statements.quote: some varieties of Mexican Guerrero Nahuatl have recently been described as having word accent in locations related to the position of a historical non-word-final coda *h. Here, the hypothesis is investigated that coda *h lowered the fundamental frequency (F0) of the tautosyllabic vowel and that a H−L pitch contour was subsequently incorporated into the lexical representation of the word as *h was weakened and lost. ... The results indicated that the new accentual patterns found in some dialects have their origin in the phonetic lowering of F0 in syllables containing coda *h.
tone_statements.summary: Penultimate accent language; some Guerrero dialects lexicalized an H-L contour from coda *h (tonogenesis in progress).

sources.citation: Mason, David. 2015. Field Notes - Grammar Outline [Guerrero Nahuatl]. Draft manuscript, 358 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives 62736.
sources.quote: No general stress rule stated. Incidental remarks consistent with penult stress over word+enclitic: 'The demonstrative pronouns may function as end clitics effecting the location of the accent. akínon who? akinón on who is that? akinón in who is this?' (p.252); 'The copula verb is an enclitic effecting the location of the accent: weyí yes it will be big, wéyi it is big' (p.338); perfect o- 'If the word is only two syllables long it must stick around to carry the accent: o-kichiw' (p.79).

sources.quote: 'El acento cae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. Sin embargo, cada dialecto del náhuatl divide algunas palabras en diferente numero de silabas. Por ejemplo: náhuatl de Guerrero ki.kóch.tia / náhuatl de Tlamacazapa ki.koch.tí.ya' — an independent SIL statement of fixed penultimate word stress for (Atliaca-area) Guerrero Nahuatl, i.e. a non-Balsas part of the [ngu] range.

sources.note: Balsas communities have a hybrid stress-and-tone system from breathy coda [ɦ]; three patterns: Ahuelicán keeps *h with a phonologized H-L contour starting on the preceding syllable, L specified on the [ɦ]-syllable, L inhibits stress (final stress shift); Oapan lost *h, keeps lexical H, tone and penult stress interact by moraic clash avoidance (rightward stress shift unless penult bimoraic), and H tone/lengthening now mark reduplication independent of *h; Ameyaltepec lost *h but has no tone, penultimate stress; Tetelcingo non-tonogenetic. Seven-village tonogenetic cluster.

sources.note: Tests the hypothesis that coda *h lowered F0 of the tautosyllabic vowel and that an H-L pitch contour was lexicalized as *h weakened/lost; four dialects, six speakers each; results: new accentual (tonal) patterns originate in F0 lowering in coda-*h syllables, and the phonologized pattern may not match the phonetic locus after *h loss. Precursor of Guion et al. 2010.
